strengths: The paper tackles an important problem: extracting global, human-readable explanations from GNNs rather than producing only instance-level feature attributions.

The combination of structural patterns, thresholded hidden activations, decision trees, and logical rules is intuitive and potentially useful. Distinguishing descriptive rules from more compact discriminative rules is also a sensible design choice.
Experiments cover three real-world graph datasets and two GNN architectures. The extracted classifier attains test accuracy close to the underlying GNN on the reported splits.
The qualitative molecular examples suggest that jointly represented motifs may expose relationships that simpler concept-based explanations overlook.
weaknesses: The central claim of a rule-based functional equivalent of the GNN is not established. The rule learner uses ground-truth labels, is trained only on correctly classified examples, and is evaluated primarily by label accuracy. No prediction-agreement/fidelity metric is reported, and the fact that the rules outperform the GNN further shows that accuracy is not evidence of functional equivalence.

The inference procedure abstains when multiple classes match, but the paper does not report coverage, abstention rate, or how such cases are treated when computing accuracy. This makes the main quantitative results difficult to interpret.

The extracted models are extremely large—up to 2,293 predicates, more than 1,000 descriptive clauses for a class, and hundreds of discriminative clauses. The paper provides no quantitative interpretability evaluation, user study, rule-length statistics, or comparison at matched fidelity, so the claim of human interpretability is weakly supported.

Grounding is underspecified and partly circular: the proposed input representation contains neighboring predicates whose definitions depend on hidden GNN embeddings. It is unclear how the fully grounded rule classifier evaluates a new graph without invoking the original GNN. For predicates lacking an isomorphic counterpart, selecting a minimum-variance or expert-chosen feature is not a principled discriminative grounding method.

The evaluation is too limited for the strength of the claims. It uses one 80/20 split with no repeated runs, uncertainty estimates, validation protocol, hyperparameter details, ablations, scalability measurements, or node-classification experiment despite claiming applicability to that setting.

Baseline comparisons are incomplete and potentially mismatched. Only GLGExplainer receives a quantitative classification comparison, GCNeuron is omitted from the table, and XGNN is compared through selected qualitative examples. Standard explanation metrics such as fidelity, sparsity, stability, and completeness are absent.

The generative-model and drug-design claims are substantially overstated. The evidence consists of selected examples, many resembling reconstruction, without measurements of validity, uniqueness, novelty, chemical valence, property preservation, distributional similarity, or performance against modern graph generators. The generation algorithm also provides no guarantee of globally consistent motifs or chemically valid graphs.

Important methodological details are missing, including the graph-hashing/isomorphism procedure and collision handling, decision-tree depth and pruning, rule simplification, treatment of negative predicates, multiclass behavior, and reproducible training settings or code. There are also inconsistencies in the description of rows versus columns of the activation matrix.

The chemistry interpretations are anecdotal and sometimes overly broad—for example, treating methyl groups as generally implying non-mutagenicity. They are not validated by domain experts, statistical enrichment tests, or controlled counterfactual analysis.

The proposed pipeline—extracting activation/structure predicates, constructing discriminative rules, and grounding them in input features—is intuitive and potentially useful. :codex-file-citation{path="/fsx/homes/Yaochen.Wang@mbzuai.ac.ae/AI-reviewer/experiments/runs/20260921_han_gpt_all_anonymized_review/scratch/f8920749aac443f1b7be2ec940cc28de/work/manuscript.pdf" purpose="source"}
The method attempts to go beyond purely descriptive explanations by constructing class-discriminative rules and exploring their use as a standalone classifier.
The presentation includes a helpful running example and reports rule cardinalities rather than hiding the resulting explanation complexity.
The reported test accuracies of the extracted classifier are close to those of the source GNN on the three evaluated datasets, suggesting that the surrogate may retain useful predictive information.
weaknesses: The central claim that the rules are a “functional equivalent” of the GNN is not supported. Rules are learned using labels and only correctly predicted training examples, while evaluation reports ground-truth accuracy rather than agreement with the GNN. No fidelity, coverage, disagreement, or ambiguous/abstention rate is reported. A finite disjunction of observed training patterns cannot establish global functional equivalence.

The inference protocol is underspecified: the paper says a prediction is made only when exactly one class rule matches, but does not explain how unmatched or multiply matched test instances are handled when computing Table 1 accuracy. This omission could materially change the main result.

The claimed interpretability is questionable. The extracted models contain up to 2,293 predicates and over 1,800 descriptive clauses, with hundreds of discriminative clauses. Many displayed rules remain opaque predicate IDs, and there is no complexity comparison, user study, or systematic evaluation showing that humans can understand them.

The grounding procedure is not technically convincing. Neighbor features include predicates that themselves depend on hidden embeddings, creating potential recursive or circular explanations rather than rules expressed solely in observable inputs. For predicates without isomorphic counterparts, selecting a feature through expert choice or minimum variance does not establish that the feature semantically defines or discriminates the predicate.

The evaluation is substantially insufficient for the claims: it uses only three datasets, one 80/20 split, no repeated trials or uncertainty, no validation protocol, no sensitivity analysis, no ablations, no runtime or scalability measurements, and no node-classification experiment despite claiming applicability to that setting.

Model agnosticism is not demonstrated convincingly: only one architecture is used per dataset, with GCN on two datasets and GraphSAGE on one. The effect of depth, pooling, hidden size, hashing choices, and decision-tree hyperparameters is unexamined.

Baseline evaluation is weak and potentially unfair. Only GLGExplainer appears in the quantitative classification table, where its near-random performance is not investigated; GCNeuron and XGNN receive only selective qualitative comparisons. Standard surrogate and rule-learning baselines are absent.

The generative claims are unsupported by quantitative evidence. The paper presents a few selected reconstructions or examples but measures neither chemical validity, novelty, uniqueness, diversity, distributional similarity, target-property preservation, nor source-GNN confidence. Consequently, claims about accurately modeling the data distribution and potential drug-design utility are premature.

Several chemistry interpretations are overgeneralized. In particular, claiming that molecules containing a methyl group are non-mutagenic is not a valid general rule, and the cited work on DNA methyltransferases does not substantiate that structural claim. There is no domain-expert validation or enrichment analysis for the discovered motifs.

The paper conflates MUTAG with the much larger Mutagenicity dataset: it describes 4,337 graphs while alternating between the names “MUTAG” and “Mutagenicity.” This ambiguity undermines reproducibility and comparison with prior results.

The method appears closely derived from the cited NEUROLOGIC approach, but the novelty beyond adapting its decision-tree rule-extraction idea to graph representations is not sharply established. Broader literature on surrogate rule extraction is also insufficiently discussed.

Key implementation details are missing, including the graph-hashing scheme and collision handling, precise construction and simplification of formulas, tree depth/pruning choices, feature preprocessing, random seeds, and complete GNN training settings. No reproducibility resources are identified.

The paper makes safety-sensitive claims about transparent drug design while offering no validation that generated molecular graphs are chemically feasible or safe. The brief impact statement acknowledges human oversight but does not address the concrete risks created by invalid rules or molecules.

strengths: The paper targets an important problem—global, human-readable explanations of GNN behavior—and proposes an intuitive pipeline combining structural patterns, hidden activations, decision trees, and logical rules.

The distinction between descriptive rules for generation and discriminative rules for classification is conceptually useful, and the worked example makes the main construction relatively easy to follow.

Experiments cover three real-world graph datasets and two GNN architectures. The extracted classifier attains test accuracy close to the source GNN, including small improvements on BBBP and Mutagenicity.
The molecular case studies illustrate how grounded rules could expose interactions between motifs that concept-level methods might overlook.
The paper discusses potential high-stakes risks and appropriately states that the method should complement rather than replace human oversight.
weaknesses: The central claim that the rules explain or are functionally equivalent to the GNN is not established. Evaluation reports accuracy against ground-truth labels rather than fidelity or agreement with the source model. Because rule construction uses class labels and correctly classified training examples, improved task accuracy does not demonstrate recovery of the GNN's reasoning.

It is unclear whether inference can actually proceed without the original GNN. Predicates depend on hidden node embeddings, while the proposed grounding procedure is informal, may use expert-selected features, and is not evaluated for completeness or fidelity. This substantially weakens the claim that the rules can replace the neural model.

The experimental evidence is too limited for the broad claims: there is only one train/test split, no repeated runs or uncertainty estimates, few quantitative baselines, and no ablations for structural hashes, embedding predicates, connectivity patterns, grounding choices, or decision-tree complexity.

Critical classifier behavior is unspecified. The method abstains when no rule or multiple classes' rules match, but the paper does not report coverage, ambiguity rates, or how such cases are handled when computing Table 1 accuracy.

The extracted models are extremely large—up to 2,293 predicates and hundreds or thousands of clauses—yet there is no quantitative readability analysis, complexity comparison, user study, or demonstration that typical predictions admit concise explanations. This challenges the interpretability claim.

The generative results are anecdotal. There are no measurements of validity, novelty, uniqueness, distributional similarity, target-property success, chemical valence, or model confidence. A handful of visual examples cannot support claims about accurately modeling the data distribution or applicability to drug design.

Several knowledge-discovery claims are based on selected examples and broad chemical interpretations rather than systematic validation. Some conclusions, such as the general association between a methyl group and non-mutagenicity, appear overly strong, and the cited evidence does not clearly establish the claimed relationship.

Reproducibility is insufficient: important GNN training settings, feature and edge preprocessing, split seeds, decision-tree hyperparameters, structural hashing details, rule simplification, grounding procedures, and generation sampling choices are missing, and no implementation is identified. Overall, the idea is promising, but the missing fidelity, grounding, statistical, and generation evaluations prevent acceptance at a top-tier venue.

strengths: The paper addresses an important problem: producing global, human-readable explanations of GNN behavior rather than only instance-level feature attributions.
The framework is conceptually interesting, combining receptive-field hashing, discretized hidden activations, decision trees, logical rules, and input-space grounding in a unified pipeline.
The empirical study covers several graph and molecular datasets, multiple GNN architectures, three-seed results, scaffold-based splits, runtime measurements, and an initial rule-stability analysis.
The method obtains strong task-label accuracy relative to the two evaluated rule-based explainers and is substantially faster in the reported experiments.

The paper includes useful qualitative examples of grounded chemical patterns and explicitly acknowledges limitations on graphs with weak structural regularity and risks from overtrusting generated molecules.
weaknesses: The central claim of being a “functionally equivalent” explanation of the GNN is not evaluated. The paper reports accuracy against ground-truth labels, but never reports agreement/fidelity to the GNN, class-conditional fidelity, or behavior on counterfactual inputs. Indeed, exceeding the GNN's label accuracy is evidence that the surrogate differs from the GNN, not that it faithfully explains it.

The extraction process is supervised using ground-truth labels Y and retains only correctly classified training examples. Consequently, the method can learn the underlying classification task instead of the GNN's decision function. This makes comparisons of task accuracy with the original GNN and claims about capturing its reasoning substantially confounded.

A key construction is mathematically unjustified: thresholds learned on mean-pooled graph embeddings are broadcast to individual node embeddings, and graph predicates are defined existentially. In general, mean_v h_v[k] >= T is not equivalent to the existence of a node with h_v[k] >= T. No approximation bound or ablation establishes that this preserves the modeled computation.

The logical semantics and prediction procedure are insufficiently specified. Descriptive clauses encode only present predicates, so multiple class rules may hold simultaneously; the paper does not clearly define conflict resolution, unseen-pattern handling, multiclass behavior, or how grounded rules yield the reported classifier predictions.

Interpretability is not convincingly established. The method produces as many as 342 clauses on Mutagenicity, many covering very few examples, while omitting core complexity measures such as numbers of predicates/literals, clause length, tree depth, compression, or human evaluation. The rule-overlap metric is also undefined, especially because independently extracted hashes and thresholds need not align across folds.

The graph-generation contribution is supported only by selected visual examples and comparison to the old XGNN method. There are no quantitative measurements of chemical validity, uniqueness, novelty, diversity, distributional similarity, property control, or GNN-target success, and no competitive modern molecular generator baselines. Thus claims of accurate distribution modeling, bonding correctness, and drug-design potential are unsupported.

Baseline coverage is narrow for the breadth of the claims. Only two rule-based explainers are used for classification, while other global/concept/surrogate approaches are omitted; node classification has no explainer baselines at all. The extensive criticism and modification of GLGExplainer further makes the comparison dependent on implementation choices that are not fully documented.

Important reproducibility details are missing, including decision-tree depth/pruning and selection, the precise graph hash and collision/isomorphism treatment, grounding-feature selection, predicate/connectivity construction, conflict handling, and generation hyperparameters. No code or complete machine-readable rules are provided.

Several secondary claims are overstated or inaccurate: graph hashing does not generally guarantee isomorphism, the stated architecture-agnostic argument does not prove generalization, the complexity discussion omits relevant dependence on predicate and tree sizes, and Cora/PubMed are described as heterogeneous graphs. Overall, the promising idea is undermined by an evaluation that does not test its defining explanation-fidelity claim.

strengths: The paper targets an important problem: producing global, human-readable explanations of graph neural networks without requiring a predefined concept vocabulary.

Combining local structural hashes, discretized hidden activations, and decision trees is intuitive and potentially useful. The framework also attempts to cover classification, knowledge extraction, and graph generation within one representation.

The empirical study spans several graph datasets and GNN architectures, reports runtime and multiple predictive metrics over three seeds, and includes additional scaffold-split and rule-stability experiments.
The paper is generally understandable and provides illustrative examples of extracted molecular patterns and rule-guided generation.
weaknesses: The central functional-equivalence claim is not supported by the methodology or evaluation. The decision trees are trained using ground-truth labels Y, and rule construction retains training instances correctly classified by the GNN. Consequently, LogicXGNN is a new supervised classifier informed by GNN embeddings, not merely an explanation of the GNN. Its ability to outperform the GNN is therefore unsurprising and does not demonstrate greater explanatory fidelity.

The primary evaluation reports accuracy against ground truth rather than agreement with the explained model. No standard fidelity, completeness, or counterfactual-faithfulness measurements are provided. A surrogate can have high task accuracy while disagreeing substantially with the GNN, so the main explanatory claim remains untested.

The claimed model agnosticism and architecture generality are overstated. The method requires internal node and graph embeddings, assumes mean pooling, and broadcasts graph-level decision-tree thresholds to individual nodes. A threshold on a mean-pooled embedding is not generally equivalent to the existence of a node crossing that threshold, so this construction does not faithfully model pooling or arbitrary GNN computations.

Grounding is insufficiently principled. For predicates without isomorphic counterparts, the explanation may be chosen using expert knowledge or simply the lowest-variance feature; neither establishes that the feature caused or is sufficient for the predicate activation. Recursive use of neighboring predicates further complicates semantics. No quantitative test shows that the grounded, human-readable rules preserve the behavior of either the hidden predicates or the GNN.

The resulting explanations are often very large: the method extracts 342 clauses for Mutagenicity and 74 for BBBP, with many clauses covering only a few instances. There is no rule-length analysis, complexity-accuracy tradeoff, user study, or comparison of interpretability. Calling these rule sets interpretable is therefore inadequately substantiated.

The experimental controls are incomplete. Important baselines such as a decision tree directly on graph embeddings, classifiers using structural fingerprints, and other global surrogate or concept methods are absent. There are also no ablations for structural hashes, activation patterns, threshold selection, connectivity patterns, or grounding, and no sensitivity analysis for tree complexity or hashing choices.

The graph-generation contribution is supported only by selected qualitative examples. The paper explicitly leaves systematic evaluation to future work and reports no validity, uniqueness, novelty, diversity, property-control, distributional, or target-GNN-score metrics. Rules are manually modified to match connectivity patterns drawn from the dataset, making the strong claims of controlled generation, chemical validity, and drug-design potential unsupported.

The chemical knowledge claims rely on visually selected patterns and post-hoc literature narratives rather than blinded expert assessment or statistical validation. Dataset correlations and artifacts are not distinguished from chemically causal or generalizable knowledge.

Several reproducibility details are missing or unclear, including the exact graph-hashing procedure, collision handling, decision-tree hyperparameters, rule simplification, unseen test-pattern handling, representative-clause selection, and the precise definition of rule overlap. The complexity analysis also omits important costs such as GNN inference, hashing receptive fields, and decision-tree training.

The node-classification experiment is especially underdeveloped: it gives only two accuracy values, incorrectly describes Cora and PubMed as heterogeneous datasets, and provides essentially no protocol or explanatory evaluation. Overall, these problems undermine the paper's main claims sufficiently to warrant rejection. strengths: The paper presents an interesting, potentially useful framework combining structural hashing, hidden-activation discretization, decision trees, and logical rules for global GNN interpretation.
The evaluation spans multiple graph datasets, GNN architectures, random seeds, an out-of-distribution setting, rule-stability analysis, and node classification.
The extracted molecular patterns are intuitive, and the reported surrogate accuracy and runtime compare favorably with the two rule-based baselines.
The distinction between compact discriminative rules and richer descriptive rules is conceptually appealing and enables applications beyond classification.
weaknesses: The central claim that LOGICXGNN explains, or is functionally equivalent to, the original GNN is not adequately supported. The method uses ground-truth labels when selecting embedding dimensions and learning discriminative rules, yet evaluation reports accuracy against ground truth rather than fidelity to the GNN's predictions. Outperforming the GNN can therefore reflect supervision from labels rather than faithful extraction of its reasoning.

No direct explanation-fidelity measurements are reported, such as prediction agreement, class-conditional fidelity, or behavior under controlled interventions. Consequently, the main interpretability claim cannot be distinguished from training a new rule-based classifier on GNN representations.

Interpretability is not evaluated rigorously. The descriptive explanations contain up to hundreds of clauses, many covering very few instances, while no rule-length, sparsity, coverage-versus-complexity, human evaluation, or comparison at matched fidelity is provided.

The generative contribution is supported only by selected qualitative examples. There are no standard measurements of chemical validity, uniqueness, novelty, diversity, property control, or agreement with the target GNN, and the comparison with XGNN is too limited to justify claims concerning accurate distribution modeling or drug-design potential.

Important ablations are missing, including the separate effects of structural hashes, activation patterns, connectivity patterns, grounding choices, and decision-tree complexity. Rule-overlap computation is also insufficiently defined.

The grounding procedure is partly heuristic: predicates without isomorphic counterparts are explained using expert-selected or minimum-variance features, neither of which establishes that the resulting feature is causally or discriminatively responsible for the GNN behavior.

The claimed logical equivalence is formally unclear. The extracted implications are not biconditionals, rules for different classes may overlap, and constructing clauses from observed training activation patterns provides no guarantee over unseen graphs.

Reproducibility is limited by missing precise settings for hashing, decision-tree regularization, rule simplification and matching, connectivity-pattern construction, and graph generation. Overall, the ideas are promising, but the evidence does not yet validate the paper's central explanation and generation claims at a top-tier standard.
